comments.comment: Where does 1.60°C come from? Name the data product and baseline so the reader can interpret the number.
You use one calendar year to declare a long-term threshold crossed. Does the WMO's definition support that inference?

decisions.response: [I1] [A1] In Estimate we now identify the source of the 1.60°C value as the Copernicus analysis of ERA5 and name its baseline.
decisions.passage: The Copernicus Climate Change Service reported warming of 1.60°C for 2024 using ERA5.

decisions.response: [I2] [B1] We removed the claim that 2024 settled the Paris Agreement threshold. Interpretation now distinguishes an annual anomaly from warming assessed over decades, as the WMO does in its bulletin.
decisions.passage: The WMO distinguishes long-term warming, measured over decades rather than an individual year, from this annual anomaly.

evidence.quote: measured over decades rather than an individual year

comments.comment: Attribution helps, but readers of the WMO bulletin will expect its consolidated 1.55 °C estimate. Replace the single-product value with that estimate and give the uncertainty.
Keep the ERA5 result. Removing it would leave the Copernicus bulletin unexplained.

comments.location: Copernicus used 1850-1900 as its estimate of the pre-industrial baseline.
comments.comment: Shouldn't the reference period for the Copernicus anomaly be 1991–2020 instead?

decisions.response: [I1] [A1] [B2] [A2] The first reply correctly attributed 1.60°C but left the WMO figure out. Rather than replace one with the other, Estimate now gives the ERA5 result alongside the WMO's 1.55 °C estimate and its ± 0.13 °C uncertainty. Interpretation explains why the two values need not coincide.
decisions.passage: For 2024, Copernicus reported 1.60°C of warming using ERA5, while the WMO consolidated six datasets and reported 1.55 °C (with a margin of uncertainty of ± 0.13 °C).

decisions.response: [I3] [B3] We retained the 1850-1900 baseline in Estimate. This is the baseline Copernicus explicitly used for its 1.60°C anomaly. Substituting 1991–2020 without changing the value would mislabel the estimate.
decisions.passage: Copernicus used 1850-1900 as its estimate of the pre-industrial baseline.
